title: Ancient fish bones reveal how Arctic cod species survived the last ice age
description: The glacial Arctic Ocean was not a barren ice desert but a breeding ground for the evolution of cold adaptation in marine fish. This is the main conclusion of a new scientific publication from Stockholm University that examines small fish bones found in deep-sea sediments during an expedition aboard the Swedish icebreaker Oden.

title: Ancient Lizard Tail in Amber Proves Voluntary Shedding Existed 99 Million Years Ago
description: In the northwestern part of the Kachin State in Myanmar, resin trees once exuded a sticky, golden liquid that trapped the insects and small animals of the Cretaceous period. For a long time, scientists viewed these entombed creatures merely as snapshots of ancient life, frozen in time but offering little insight into how these animals actually lived. That perspective shifted with the discovery of an eight-millimeter fragment preserved within a piece of Burmese amber. It is a piece of a lizard's tail, and it changes our understanding of ancient reptilian behavior in a tangible way. The fragment, dated to approximately 99 million years ago, represents the first direct evidence that ancient lizards possessed the ability to voluntarily shed their tails as a defense mechanism. Known as caudal autotomy, this trait allows a lizard to detach its tail when grabbed by a predator. The severed tail continues to writhe, acting as a living decoy that distracts the attacker while the animal escapes. While we have long assumed this behavior existed in the deep past, finding physical proof of it was a significant hurdle for paleontologists. The challenge lay in the nature of the fossil record. Before this discovery, scientists could only rely on indirect evidence. Fossilized vertebrae sometimes showed "fracture lines" or weak planes-structural weak points where a tail could break. However, the presence of these weak points did not confirm the animal's capability to actively trigger the separation. Without preserved soft tissues, it was impossible to distinguish between a tail that broke due to a predator's force and one that was shed through a complex physiological act.
